newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross reports on Nazi allegations.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross reports on Nazi allegations.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross said on Monday it found three cases of misconduct by former employees in an investigation on claims that it had been penetrated by Nazi agents during World War Two.

U.S. wartime intelligence documents declassified last year claimed the Swiss-run agency was used as a cover for Nazi agents and that some of its employees used their position to carry enemy funds and enemy-owned jewels across the Swiss border.

The Geneva-based ICRC, defender of war victims and political prisoners around the globe, said its own investigation revealed that only 18 people among 49 named in the documents unearthed by the World Jewish Congress had worked for it during the war.

Three of them, Giuseppe Beretta, Jean-Roger Pagan and Jean Sublet, appeared to have been involved in "more or less serious cases of individual misconduct" but charges against the other 15 stemmed from ignorance of the ICRC's role and activities, it said in a statement late Monday.
Neutral Switzerland's financial ties to Nazi Germany have been at the centre of a controversy over Jewish charges that its banks profitted from unclaimed bank accounts of murdered Jews.
The U.S. documents said Beretta, an ICRC official in Turkey in 1945, was found by police there to have gold coins he had been given by a German Nazi agent.
The ICRC said it had dismissed Beretta in the light of its suspicions but that there was no proof that he had made wrongful use of ICRC's mail service to transfer funds or valuables.

A second case concerned Swissman Pagan who had worked at the ICRC Geneva for a year in 1941-42 but resigned and went to North Africa where he was arrested by the Free French authorities in 1943 and shot for spying for the Germans a year later.
The ICRC said Pagan had allegedly admitted he had been recruited by German spies to pass on information on the Allies.

The third case involved Sublet, assigned by the ICRC in Algiers to work as a volunteer in Tangiers in 1944 and accused of having passed on information to the Germans. He was sacked after the ICRC became aware of the charges against him, it said.
